shortDescription: In Carthage and Hippo, in Roman Africa, Latin-speaking Christians gathered around one bishop. He taught them, cared for their poor, judged their quarrels, and decided with them when to take back those who had fallen away.

timeline.headline: Decius's persecution reaches Carthage, and Cyprian leads his church by letter from hiding
timeline.witness: Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, in his own letters

lines.text: The emperor Decius begins a persecution of the churches.
Under an edict ordering the people to sacrifice, the crowd at Carthage, in the circus and the amphitheater, again and again calls for Cyprian to be thrown to the lion.

Because the people keep shouting violently for him, Cyprian withdraws, he writes, for his people's peace, so that his presence will not stir the riot further. Absent in body, he keeps up his counsel to them.
The clergy of Rome write to the clergy of Carthage that Cyprian has withdrawn and acted rightly, and remind them that the hired man who is no shepherd leaves the sheep when the wolf comes.
lines.reference: The Roman clergy, Letter 2 in the English, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 28796-28800, 28816-28820
lines.note: The Roman clergy's letter, which Cyprian answers.

lines.text: From hiding, he asks his clergy to see that nothing is lacking for the confessors in prison or for the poor who stand firm, since the church's small fund has been shared out among the clergy for such needs.

The brothers are to visit the confessors with care and not in crowds, and the priests who offer the Eucharist in the prison are to take turns, each with one deacon, so the changing faces draw less ill will.
He tells his clergy he cannot answer them alone: from his first days as bishop he resolved to do nothing on his own judgment without their counsel and the people's consent.
Many, he writes, did not wait to be arrested, but ran to the marketplace of their own accord to sacrifice.
lines.reference: Cyprian, On the Lapsed 8, cic/texts/cyprian_de-lapsis-lat_hartel1868-csel3-tei.txt lines 345-351; English, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 43828-43838

lines.text: Until peace returns to the church, he writes, the bishops, meeting with the clergy and with the people who stood firm, are to settle everything by common counsel.

timeline.headline: The bishops decide on the fallen, and a rival bishop is set up at Rome

lines.text: A large number of bishops meet and choose a middle way: the fallen are not wholly denied the hope of peace, but their penance is long, and each case is examined.
Cyprian holds that no one should be barred from penance and the hope of peace, since sinners are called back to repent, and pardon is not refused the penitent.
The party of Novatian at Rome, Cyprian reports, says that one is stained by another's sin, by sharing communion with the fallen.
lines.note: Their view, as Cyprian reports it.

lines.text: Envoys of Novatian come to Carthage with word that he has been made bishop. Cyprian and the bishops with him at once keep them from communion, since he was made bishop against the Catholic Church.
At the assembly the envoys burst in with insults and shouting, and demand that their charges be heard in public. The bishops refuse.
They go on from house to house and town to town, trying to split the church.

timeline.headline: Plague strikes, and Carthage ransoms captives

lines.text: A dreadful plague strikes. People flee the sick and leave their own, and the dead lie throughout the city.
lines.reference: Pontius, Life of Cyprian 9, cic/texts/cyprian_opera-spuria-vita-pontius-lat_hartel-csel3-pars3.txt lines 40783-40793; English, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 27940-27955

lines.text: Cyprian gathers the people and teaches them that it is nothing great to care only for their own, and that the perfect love even their enemies.
lines.reference: Pontius, Life of Cyprian 9, cic/texts/cyprian_opera-spuria-vita-pontius-lat_hartel-csel3-pars3.txt lines 40797-40804; English, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 27961-27967

lines.text: The tasks are shared out by rank and station, and the poor, who have no money to give, give their own work. Good is done for all, and not only for the household of faith.
lines.reference: Pontius, Life of Cyprian 10, cic/texts/cyprian_opera-spuria-vita-pontius-lat_hartel-csel3-pars3.txt lines 40848-40856; English, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 27981-27990

lines.text: Christian men, women and consecrated virgins of Numidia are carried off by raiders. Cyprian writes to the Numidian bishops that their captivity must be counted as his church's own.
Carthage sends a hundred thousand sesterces, gathered from its clergy and people, to ransom them, and Cyprian sends the givers' names so the Numidians can pray for them.

timeline.headline: Cyprian and Stephen of Rome disagree over baptism

lines.text: Cyprian quotes Stephen, bishop of Rome: those who come from any heresy are to have hands laid on them for repentance, and nothing new is to be done. Cyprian calls this Stephen's error.

timeline.headline: Cyprian is exiled, then tried and beheaded
timeline.witness: The Acta, the record of Cyprian's trials and death

lines.text: The proconsul tells Cyprian that the emperors Valerian and Gallienus have ordered those who do not keep the Roman religion to take part in the Roman rites. Cyprian answers that he is a Christian and a bishop, and is sent into exile at Curubis.

lines.when: on the Ides of September, when Tuscus and Bassus were consuls
lines.text: Officers come to bring him back. He is held at an officer's house, and all his people gather in the street outside the door, where he has the girls looked after.

lines.when: the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October
lines.text: Before the proconsul Galerius Maximus he refuses to sacrifice. The sentence calls him an enemy of the Roman gods and of their sacred rites, and the leader of men gathered in a wicked conspiracy, and orders him put to the sword. He answers, Thanks be to God.

The brothers cry out that they will be beheaded with him. He is led out, the brothers lay cloths before him, a priest and a subdeacon bind his eyes, and he is beheaded. By night his body is carried with candles and torches to burial.
Jerome writes that Pontius, Cyprian's deacon, shared his exile up to the day of his death, and left a fine book on his life and death.
lines.note: Jerome wrote more than a century later.

timeline.headline: A rival church rises at Carthage
timeline.witness: Optatus, a Catholic bishop who wrote against the rival church sixty years and more after the persecution

lines.text: By the vote of the whole people, Caecilian is chosen bishop of Carthage.
lines.reference: Optatus, Against the Donatists I.18, cic/texts/optatus_against-the-donatists.txt line 207

lines.text: His enemies charge that the bishop who consecrated him had handed over the Scriptures in the persecution. Optatus calls the charge false.
lines.reference: Optatus, Against the Donatists I.19, cic/texts/optatus_against-the-donatists.txt line 217
lines.note: An enemy's account of the charge.

lines.text: A rival party makes Majorinus bishop, although Caecilian is already bishop, and altar is raised against altar.
lines.reference: Optatus, Against the Donatists I.15, I.19, cic/texts/optatus_against-the-donatists.txt lines 187, 229; Latin, cic/texts/optatus_libri-vii-lat_ziwsa1893-csel26-tei.txt line 989

lines.text: The rival church's bishop Parmenian holds that one who is stained cannot wash away sins in baptism.
lines.reference: Optatus, Against the Donatists I.10, cic/texts/optatus_against-the-donatists.txt line 153; Latin, cic/texts/optatus_libri-vii-lat_ziwsa1893-csel26-tei.txt lines 589-590
lines.note: Parmenian's words, as his opponent quotes them.

lines.when: "sixty years and more" after the persecution
lines.text: Optatus writes that the rival side are schismatics, outside the Catholic Church, who yet share its true sacraments. Heretics, to him, are those who have falsified the creed.
lines.reference: Optatus, Against the Donatists I.10-13, cic/texts/optatus_against-the-donatists.txt lines 143, 155, 169, 177

timeline.when: While Augustine is a priest at Hippo
timeline.headline: Augustine is made a priest, and pleads with his people over the feast they call the Gladness
timeline.witness: Augustine, in his own letters and books, and Possidius, his friend and fellow bishop

lines.text: Valerius, bishop of Hippo, asks the people to find a priest for the city. They lay hold of Augustine, standing among them, and bring him to be ordained while he weeps. He later says he foresaw the dangers of governing the church.
The people will not bear the ban on a feast in the church they call the Gladness, which, Augustine writes, hides drunkenness under its name.
He reads them Scripture against drunkenness and pleads with them by Christ's sufferings and by the love of their old bishop. They weep, and he weeps with them.
Some still ask why the feast is forbidden now, since those before them who allowed it were Christians.
He tells them, as he understands it, that after the persecutions the church's forebears let newcomers keep feasts for the martyrs in place of the idol feasts they gave up.
They hear from the church of the heretics the noise of its usual feasting. In their own church, a great number of men and women stay singing hymns until the light fails.
At Hasna, he writes, men he calls Circumcelliones break into the church and smash the altar, and the case is before the courts.
He writes a psalm against the party of Donatus for the plainest people to sing and remember, one verse for each letter of the Latin alphabet.

timeline.when: While Augustine is bishop of Hippo
timeline.headline: The bishop preaches, judges and gives
timeline.witness: Possidius, Augustine's friend and fellow bishop, and Augustine's own writings

lines.text: Possidius writes that the Catholic church in Africa had long lain low, while the rebaptizing party of Donatus held a large multitude of Africans, some of them living in Hippo and the towns nearby.
Augustine preaches at home and in church, and people of the rival church come with the Catholics to hear him, bringing writers to take down what he says.
He hears the cases of Christians and of men of any sect, since Paul told believers not to go to law before unbelievers, sometimes until mealtime and sometimes fasting all day.
When the church's money runs out, he tells the people he has nothing to give the poor, and for captives and the needy has the church's sacred vessels broken up and melted down.
Deogratias, a deacon of Carthage to whom newcomers are brought for their first teaching in the faith, asks Augustine to write him how to teach them.

At first, Augustine writes, he wanted the rival church won by argument only. Then his fellow bishops pointed to his own town, once wholly for Donatus and brought over by fear of the emperors' laws, and he gave way. Those laws punished the rival church with exile and fines.

He preaches at Carthage that where a savage crowd once gathered to shed Cyprian's blood, a crowd now gathers to honor him, at a table built for God and called Cyprian's table, because there he was offered.

timeline.headline: The Vandals overrun Africa, and Augustine dies in besieged Hippo

lines.text: Vandals and Alans, with some Goths and other peoples, cross by ship from Spain and overrun Africa. Of countless churches, only those of Carthage, Hippo and Cirta still stand, and the hymns and praises of God perish from the churches.

A fellow bishop, Honoratus, writes to ask whether bishops and clergy should leave their churches as the enemy approaches. Augustine answers that one who is sought in particular may flee, but when the danger is common to all, those who need the clergy must not be left by them.

If the clergy are there, he writes, all are helped: some are baptized, others reconciled, and none is cheated of communion. Possidius copies the letter into his Life as very useful, even necessary, for priests.
The Vandals besiege Hippo for almost fourteen months. Possidius and other bishops take refuge there.

lines.when: "in the third month of the siege"
lines.text: Augustine falls ill with fever. Up to his last illness he preaches in the church with a clear mind.

lines.when: the fifth day before the Kalends of September, when Theodosius and Valentinian were consuls
lines.text: Augustine dies, aged seventy-six, Possidius says, almost forty years of them as priest or bishop.
lines.reference: Prosper, Chronicle, cic/texts/prosper_chronica-minora-1-lat_mommsen1892.txt lines 54204-54208; Possidius, Life of Augustine 31, cic/texts/possidius_vita-augustini_weiskotten1919.txt lines 4919-4920

lines.text: Hippo, abandoned by its people, is burned by the enemy.

timeline.headline: Carthage falls, and later Africans remember Cyprian and Augustine

lines.text: Gaiseric takes Carthage by a trick of peace.
Procopius writes that the people of Carthage revere Cyprian above all others, and keep a festival called the Cypriana at his church by the sea, which the Vandals took from the Christians.
lines.reference: Procopius, History of the Wars III.21, cic/texts/procopius_wars-3-4-vandalic_dewing1916.txt lines 2206-2214

lines.text: Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, calls Cyprian bishop of Carthage and martyr, and Augustine the most wise and most famous teacher of the churches of Christ.
lines.reference: Facundus, In Defense of the Three Chapters, cic/texts/facundus-ferrandus-caesarius-dionysius-pl67-lat_migne1865.txt lines 42540-42541, 43120-43121

lines.text: In Geneva, Calvin writes that he could fill a whole book from Augustine on God's choice of whom to call.

uncertain: Cyprian's withdrawal in 250. His own letters give his reason: the crowd kept shouting for him, and he left for his people's peace, so as not to stir the riot further, and led them by letter. The Roman clergy's letter on the hired man who leaves the sheep, and his deacon Pontius's long defense, show that the withdrawal was questioned.

The charge behind the split at Carthage. The rival side said that the bishop who had made Caecilian bishop had handed over the Scriptures to be burned. Optatus, a Catholic bishop writing some sixty years later, says the charge was false, and quotes a hearing that cleared that bishop, Felix. The old sources give the split no year beyond soon after the great persecution.

The rival church speaks only through its enemies. Its own rule, that one who was stained could not wash away sins, survives in Optatus's quotation of its bishop Parmenian. Possidius says that in Augustine's early years the rebaptizing Donatist party held a large multitude of the Africans, while the Catholic church had long lain prostrate.

Who the heretics were at the Gladness. Augustine's letter says only that the sound of feasting came from the church of the heretics. That they were the Donatists rests on Possidius, who says Donatists lived in Hippo and the towns nearby. Optatus used the word differently: he called the Donatists schismatics, who had gone outside the church yet shared its true sacraments, and kept heretics for those who taught falsely about God.
The plague. Its account rests on Pontius, Cyprian's deacon and admirer, who says that people fled the sick and left their own, and that the dead lay through the whole city.

Several dates rest on modern reckoning, not on the old sources: Cyprian's election as bishop, the year of the plague, the years Augustine was made priest and bishop, and the years of his letters on the Gladness and on staying with the people.

quotationOriginals.modern: I did not move their tears with my own. But as these things were said, I confess, their weeping came first, and I could not hold back mine. When we had wept together, my sermon ended in the fullest hope that they would mend their ways.
quotationOriginals.printed: non ego illorum lacrimas meis lacrimis moui, sed cum talia dicerentur, fateor, eorum fletu praeuentus meum abstinere non potui, et cum iam pariter fleuissemus, plenissima spe correctionis illorum finis sermonis mei factus est.
quotationOriginals.work: Augustine, Letter 29.7, to Alypius (ed. A. Goldbacher, CSEL 34, 1895)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The scan prints a stray mark, a misread line number, before plenissima; it is left out here.
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: I did not move them to weep by first weeping myself; but while these things were being spoken, I own that, moved by the tears which they began to shed, I myself could not refrain from following their example. And when we had thus wept together, I concluded my sermon with full persuasion that they would be restrained by it from the abuses denounced.

quotationOriginals.modern: I could not write back alone. From my first days as bishop I resolved to do nothing on my own private judgment, without your counsel and the people's consent.
quotationOriginals.printed: solus rescribere nihil potui, quando a primordio episcopatus mei statuerim nihil sine consilio uestro et sine consensu plebis mea priuatim sententia gerere.
quotationOriginals.work: Cyprian, Letter 14.4, to his priests and deacons, 250 (ed. W. Hartel, CSEL 3.2, 1871)
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: I have not been able to reply by myself, since, from the first commencement of my episcopacy, I made up my mind to do nothing on my own private opinion, without your advice and without the consent of the people.

quotationOriginals.modern: But if the clergy are there, everyone is helped, as far as the Lord gives them strength. Some are baptized, others are reconciled. No one is cheated of communion in the Lord's body. All are comforted, built up and urged to ask God, who has the power to turn away all that is feared.
quotationOriginals.printed: Si autem ministri adsint, pro viribus quas eis Dominus subministrat, omnibus subvenitur; alii baptizantur, alii reconciliantur, nulli Dominici corporis communione fraudantur, omnes consolantur, aedificantur, exhortantur, ut Deum rogent, qui potens est omnia quae timentur avertere
quotationOriginals.work: Augustine, Letter 228.8, to Honoratus, as Possidius copies it in his Life of Augustine (ed. and tr. H. T. Weiskotten, 1919)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Words broken across lines are joined, and a misread line number inside the span is left out. Goldbacher's Latin of the letter agrees. Ministri is the clergy.
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: But if the ministers are present they are a help to all, according to the strength which the Lord gives them : some are baptized, others are reconciled, none are deprived of the communion of the body of the Lord, all are consoled, edified and exhorted to ask of God, who hath the power to avert all the things they fear
